comments.author: @cdr29qm
comments.text: For sectors where costs are rising far faster than average wages, Baumol's cost disease is an inadequate explanation.  Generic rising wages can only explain why labour-intensive services cost *the same number of hours of wages* as they did 25 years ago (contrasting with goods that have got much cheaper), not why they cost twice as many.  For the latter, you'd need other factors, like: a) workers in that sector have experienced unusually high pay raises compared to other workers; b) productivity has actually declined, i.e. more work is needed to deliver the same level of service (e.g. due to corporate bloat, regulatory burden, newer cohorts of workers are less competent than previous generations, etc); c) it's not a like-for-like comparison as the service quality has gone up (which requires more hours worked to deliver, etc); d) there is more profit margin than there used to be; e) despite being labour-intensive, the cost *increase* is being driven by non-labour costs.
